questions.stem: A swimmer puts on sunscreen to block UV light. The ozone layer, which also blocks UV, is in which atmospheric layer?
questions.explanation: Most ozone is found in the stratosphere at about 20-30 km. It absorbs UV light, which is why this layer warms with height.

questions.stem: A swim coach checks the weather before an outdoor meet. In which atmospheric layer does almost all weather happen?
questions.explanation: The troposphere holds most of the air and nearly all the water vapor, so clouds, rain and storms form here.

questions.stem: A chef boils soup in a mountain village at high altitude. The water boils below 100 °C because the

choices.E: air is colder so the soup cannot heat

questions.explanation: Water boils when its vapor pressure equals the air pressure. Higher up, air pressure is lower, so the boiling point is lower.

questions.stem: On a mountain map (suppose) the air cools by 6.5 °C for every kilometer. If it is 20 °C at the base, what is the temperature at the 8 km summit?
Which boundary between layers is the coldest place in the atmosphere (roughly -85 to -90 °C)?
questions.explanation: Temperature falls through the mesosphere and reaches its lowest value, roughly -85 to -90 °C, at the mesopause (about 85 km).

questions.stem: The International Space Station orbits about 400 km above Earth. In which layer is it?
questions.explanation: The thermosphere extends from about 85 km to about 600 km. The ISS and the aurora are in this layer.

questions.stem: Air pressure at sea level is 1013 hPa and it roughly halves every 5.5 km. About what is the pressure at 16.5 km?
The thermosphere can reach 1500 °C, yet an astronaut outside would not feel burned by the air. The best reason is that the air there

choices.A: is so thin that it transfers almost no heat
choices.C: is protected by the ozone layer
choices.D: is actually colder than the astronaut

questions.explanation: Temperature measures the speed of the few molecules. With so few particles per cubic meter, almost no heat energy is passed on.

questions.stem: Practice at an outdoor pool is stopped by a sudden thunderstorm, and the air turns cooler. Which front usually brings brief heavy showers and thunderstorms?
questions.explanation: A cold front is steep and fast, so it lifts the warm air quickly. That makes tall cumulonimbus clouds and storms.

questions.stem: In the Northern Hemisphere, winds around a low-pressure center blow

choices.A: straight into the center without turning

questions.explanation: Air flows inward toward low pressure and the Coriolis effect turns it to the right, giving a counterclockwise spiral.

questions.stem: A continental polar (cP) air mass is
questions.explanation: 'Continental' means it formed over land (dry). 'Polar' means it formed in cold high latitudes.

questions.stem: A swimmer notices a cold front has passed the pool: the wind shifted and it got cooler. What will the barometer most likely do next?
questions.explanation: Behind a cold front the cold, dense air is heavier, so pressure rises and the skies clear.

questions.stem: A warm front has a slope of 1 : 200. The warm air is 2 km above the ground. How far ahead of the surface front is that point?
questions.explanation: A 1 : 200 slope means 200 units across for every 1 up. 2 km × 200 = 400 km. That is why warm fronts bring rain far ahead of them.

questions.stem: Steam rises from a pot on the stove, so the pressure at the surface directly under the rising air tends to be lower. In the atmosphere, what do surface winds do near a region of rising air?

choices.C: Blow in a perfect circle without moving inward

questions.explanation: Rising air leaves a lower surface pressure. Air flows from higher to lower pressure, so winds converge toward the low.

questions.stem: A cold front moves at 40 km/h and a warm front 300 km ahead of it moves at 25 km/h in the same direction. How long until the cold front catches up?
questions.explanation: The cold front gains 40 - 25 = 15 km/h. Time = 300 ÷ 15 = 20 hours. Then they form an occluded front.

questions.stem: At a beach in Australia (Southern Hemisphere), what is the usual wind pattern around a low-pressure system?
questions.explanation: The Coriolis effect turns air to the left in the Southern Hemisphere, so the spiral around a low is reversed: clockwise and inward.

questions.stem: A kitchen's air holds 6 g of water vapor per cubic meter. At this temperature it could hold at most 12 g. What is the relative humidity?
On a cool evening beside the pool, the air cools but gains no water vapor. Its relative humidity
questions.explanation: Cooler air can hold less vapor, so the same vapor is closer to the maximum. RH goes up.

questions.stem: A cook notices that the herbs on a window sill make the air damp. Which process is the release of water vapor from plant leaves?
questions.explanation: Plants take water in through roots and release vapor through stomata in leaves. This is transpiration.

questions.stem: A glass of cold lemonade 'sweats' on a hot day. Why?

choices.A: The lemonade evaporates through the glass
choices.B: The glass is cooled below the dew point of the surrounding air
choices.C: Hot air has no water vapor
choices.E: The glass absorbs heat and makes water

questions.explanation: Air touching the cold glass cools below its dew point, so vapor condenses into droplets on the outside.

questions.stem: Cloud base height can be estimated as 125 m for every °C between air temperature and dew point. The air is 28 °C and the dew point is 18 °C. Where is the cloud base?
The pool water level drops a little every day without any leak. Evaporation is fastest when the air is
questions.explanation: Heat gives molecules energy to escape. Dry air can take more vapor, and wind removes the vapor above the water.

questions.stem: Air at 30 °C has relative humidity 40%. The air can hold at most 30.4 g/m³ at 30 °C and 9.4 g/m³ at 10 °C. If it cools to 10 °C, how much vapor condenses per m³?
questions.explanation: Vapor = 0.40 × 30.4 = 12.2 g/m³. At 10 °C the air can hold only 9.4 g/m³, so 12.2 - 9.4 ≈ 2.8 g condenses.

questions.stem: A cook cuts open hailstones found after a storm: they have layers like an onion. This happens because they

choices.A: melt and refreeze at sea level
choices.B: are made of compressed snow flakes only
choices.C: freeze all at once on the ground
choices.D: form when rain passes through warm air
choices.E: are carried up and down in the updraft of a thunderstorm, adding ice layers

questions.explanation: In a strong updraft a stone repeatedly passes through supercooled water, which freezes on it in layers until it is too heavy to be held up.

questions.stem: In the Hadley cell, where does the air rise?
questions.explanation: Strong sunshine heats the equator, so air rises there. It moves poleward aloft and sinks near 30°.

questions.stem: On a Valorant map (suppose) a flag shows a westerly wind. It blows from the
questions.explanation: Winds are named after the direction they come from, so a westerly blows from the west toward the east.

questions.stem: At which latitude is the Coriolis effect zero?
questions.explanation: The Coriolis effect depends on the sine of latitude. It is zero at the equator and largest at the poles.

questions.stem: A Valorant map is set in a desert near 30° N. Which feature of the circulation helps explain deserts at that latitude?

choices.A: Dry air sinking in the Hadley cell
choices.D: The ITCZ passing overhead all year
choices.E: Moist air rising in the polar cell

questions.explanation: At about 30° air sinks, warms and dries, which gives high pressure and clear skies. Many big deserts lie in this belt.

questions.stem: At a tropical beach in the Northern Hemisphere, the steady trade wind blows from the
questions.explanation: Air flows toward the equator (south). The Coriolis effect turns it right, so it comes from the northeast.

questions.stem: Soup in a pot rises in the middle, spreads at the top, cools, and sinks at the edges. In the atmosphere, which part is like the rising middle of the soup?

choices.A: The air sinking at the poles
choices.D: The air rising at the equator (ITCZ)
choices.E: The air at the Ferrel cell's top only

questions.explanation: Both are convection. Hot fluid rises where heated most. The equator is the hottest region, so air rises there.

questions.stem: Which statement about the Ferrel cell is correct?

choices.A: It is driven by direct heating at the equator
choices.B: It is driven by its neighbors and has rising air at about 60° and sinking air at about 30°
choices.C: It carries surface air from the poles to the equator
choices.D: It has rising air at 30° and sinking air at 60°

questions.explanation: The Ferrel cell is an indirect cell that sits between the Hadley and polar cells. Its surface air flows poleward (the westerlies).

questions.stem: A ship sails from the Southern Hemisphere at 20° S toward the equator and the wind is a steady trade wind. Which direction does the wind come from?
questions.explanation: Air flows from 30° S toward the equator (north). In the Southern Hemisphere the Coriolis effect turns it left, so it comes from the southeast.

questions.stem: A swim meet is called off when tall dark clouds build up. Which cloud type produces thunderstorms?
questions.explanation: Cumulonimbus clouds are tall clouds with strong updrafts that produce lightning, thunder, hail and heavy showers.

questions.stem: The calm center of a hurricane is called the
questions.explanation: In the eye, air sinks and skies are often clear. The strongest winds are in the eyewall around it.

questions.stem: On a beach camping trip at night, the wind near the coast usually blows from the
questions.explanation: Land cools faster at night, so the sea is warmer. Air rises over the warmer sea and cooler land air flows out: a land breeze.

questions.stem: During El Niño, which change usually happens in the Pacific?

choices.A: Indonesia gets more rain than usual
choices.B: Trade winds weaken and warm water spreads east
choices.D: Trade winds strengthen and the west becomes cooler

questions.explanation: Weaker trade winds let the warm pool move east, so upwelling off Peru shuts down and rain shifts east. Indonesia becomes dry.

questions.stem: Afternoon thunderstorms are common on tropical coasts. A good reason is that

choices.A: the Moon pulls the clouds up
choices.B: the sea breeze ends at noon
choices.C: ozone breaks up in the afternoon
choices.D: the warm, humid ground heats air strongly so it rises quickly
choices.E: the air is coldest in the afternoon

questions.explanation: Strong daytime heating makes moist air rise rapidly (convection), building tall cumulonimbus clouds.

questions.stem: A hurricane forms only over ocean water warmer than about
questions.explanation: Warm water supplies the heat and moisture that power a hurricane. Over cooler water or land it weakens.

questions.stem: Hurricanes almost never form within about 5° of the equator because

choices.A: the Coriolis effect there is too weak to start the spin
choices.B: the trade winds are too strong

questions.explanation: A storm needs the Coriolis effect to start rotating. It is nearly zero at the equator.

questions.stem: Why does a hurricane weaken quickly after it moves over land?

choices.D: The eye closes because of gravity
choices.E: It loses its supply of warm water and friction slows its winds

questions.explanation: A hurricane is powered by heat and moisture from warm ocean water. Over land that supply ends and friction is greater.

questions.stem: River discharge is found by multiplying cross-section area by
questions.explanation: Q = A × v. Discharge is the volume of water passing a point each second, in m³/s.

questions.stem: A fan-shaped deposit of sediment where a river meets the sea is a
questions.explanation: The river slows in the sea and drops its sediment, building a delta.

questions.stem: On a river bend, erosion is strongest on the
questions.explanation: Water flows fastest on the outside of a bend, so it cuts the bank there (a cut bank). Deposition happens on the inside (point bar).

questions.stem: A river is 12 m wide, has an average depth of 1.5 m and flows at 0.8 m/s. What is its discharge?
A tap delivers 0.15 L of water every second. A cook fills a 6 L pot. How long does it take?
questions.explanation: Discharge is volume per time. Time = 6 L ÷ 0.15 L/s = 40 s.

questions.stem: A 25 m × 10 m pool is 2 m deep (500 m³). A stream with a discharge of 0.5 m³/s is used to fill it. About how long does it take?
A river has a discharge of 60 m³/s, is 20 m wide and flows at 1.5 m/s. What is its average depth?
questions.explanation: A = Q ÷ v = 60 ÷ 1.5 = 40 m². Depth = A ÷ width = 40 ÷ 20 = 2 m.

questions.stem: After a storm the same river rises from 2 m to 3 m deep (still 20 m wide) and its velocity increases from 1.5 m/s to 2.0 m/s. By what factor does the discharge change?
questions.explanation: Before: 20 × 2 × 1.5 = 60 m³/s. After: 20 × 3 × 2.0 = 120 m³/s. That is twice as much.

questions.stem: A swimmer tastes salt in the sea. The average salinity of the oceans is about

choices.B: 35 g of salt per kg of seawater

questions.explanation: Seawater is about 3.5% salt by mass, which is 35 parts per thousand (35 g per kg).

questions.stem: A lifeguard warns of very high high tides and very low low tides. These spring tides occur at
questions.explanation: At new and full moon the Sun, Moon and Earth line up and their tidal pulls add together.

questions.stem: Lifeguards on a beach learn that most tsunamis are caused by
questions.explanation: A sudden vertical movement of the sea floor pushes up a huge volume of water and starts the waves.

questions.stem: Waves in a pool pass a lane marker 2 times every second (f = 2 Hz). The crests are 0.5 m apart. How fast do the waves travel?
A tsunami crosses an ocean 4000 m deep. Use v = √(g × d) with g = 9.8 m/s². About how fast is it?
A cook boils away 3.0 kg of seawater (salinity 35 g per kg) to make sea salt. How much salt remains?
questions.explanation: Salt = 3.0 kg × 35 g/kg = 105 g.

questions.stem: The Gulf Stream is a

choices.A: cold current moving south along the west coast of North America
choices.B: warm current moving north along the east coast of North America
choices.D: warm current in the Indian Ocean only

questions.explanation: It carries warm tropical water north and then east across the Atlantic. It is part of the North Atlantic gyre.

questions.stem: A tsunami has a wavelength of 200 km and travels at 200 m/s in the deep ocean. What is its period?
Why does surface water sink in the North Atlantic and start the deep conveyor belt?

choices.C: It is cold and salty, so it is dense
choices.D: It is warm and fresh, so it is dense

questions.explanation: Cooling and sea-ice formation make surface water colder and saltier, so denser. Dense water sinks.

questions.stem: An icy Valorant map (suppose) has a wide valley with a flat floor and steep sides (a U shape). Real valleys like this are mostly made by
questions.explanation: A glacier fills the whole valley and scours the bottom and sides, making a U shape. Rivers cut V-shaped valleys.

questions.stem: A glacier grows when

choices.D: melting is more than snow accumulation
choices.E: snow accumulation is more than melting

questions.explanation: Mass balance = accumulation - ablation. A positive balance makes the glacier thicker and it advances.

questions.stem: A ridge of rock debris dropped at the front of a glacier is a
questions.explanation: At the snout, the ice melts and drops the rock it carried, forming a terminal moraine.

questions.stem: A glacier gains 2.5 m of ice (water equivalent) per year and loses 3.1 m per year. What is the mass balance?

choices.A: 0 m per year, so it is stable
choices.B: +0.6 m per year, so it advances
choices.C: -0.6 m per year, so the glacier retreats

questions.explanation: Balance = 2.5 - 3.1 = -0.6 m per year. A negative balance means the glacier shrinks and retreats.

questions.stem: An ice cube floats in a glass of water with about 90% under the surface. Glacier ice (917 kg/m³) in sea water (1025 kg/m³) has what fraction of an iceberg underwater?
questions.explanation: Fraction submerged = density of ice ÷ density of seawater = 917 ÷ 1025 ≈ 0.89.

questions.stem: On a Valorant map with a frozen region, suppose a glacier gains 4 m of snow-equivalent and loses 3 m each year. What will probably happen?

choices.B: It will melt away at once

questions.explanation: The balance is +1 m per year, so the glacier slowly thickens and its front advances.

questions.stem: A cook drops ice cubes into a glass. Which melting will raise global sea level the most?

choices.A: Ice sheets on land such as Greenland
choices.C: Icebergs already floating in the sea
choices.D: Floating ice cubes in a glass
choices.E: Floating sea ice in the Arctic

questions.explanation: Floating ice already displaces its own mass of water. Land ice adds new water to the ocean.

questions.stem: Ice at the equilibrium line moves 80 m per year toward the terminus 4 km away. About how long does it take to arrive?
questions.explanation: Time = distance ÷ speed = 4000 m ÷ 80 m/yr = 50 years.

questions.stem: A swimmer digs a hole on the beach and finds water at some depth. The top of the zone where all pores are filled with water is the
questions.explanation: Below the water table the rock is saturated (all pores full). Above it the pores contain air and some water.

questions.stem: A kitchen sponge of 100 cm³ has 30 cm³ of empty pore space. Treat it like a rock sample: its porosity is
Which material is most likely to be an aquitard?
questions.explanation: Clay has tiny pores, so water moves through it extremely slowly.

questions.stem: A saturated sand layer is 2 m thick over an area of 100 m² and has a porosity of 25%. How much water does it hold?
questions.explanation: Volume of sand = 2 × 100 = 200 m³. Water = 0.25 × 200 = 50 m³.

questions.stem: A cook pours the same amount of water on a bowl of dry rice and on a bowl of flour. The water passes quickly through the rice but not the flour. In geology, the rice is like a layer with higher
questions.explanation: Rice has larger connected gaps, like gravel. Flour has tiny pores that block flow, like clay.

questions.stem: In an artesian well, water rises above the top of the aquifer because

choices.A: capillary action pulls it up 50 m
choices.D: the aquifer is confined and the water is under pressure

questions.explanation: A confined aquifer sealed by aquitards receives water from a higher recharge area. That pressure pushes water up the well.

questions.stem: Sample A (clay) has porosity 40%. Sample B (sand) has porosity 25%. Which supplies more water to a well, and why?

choices.B: B, because water can flow through it much more easily
choices.E: A, because its porosity is higher

questions.explanation: A well needs water to flow to it, which depends on permeability. Sand has high permeability. Clay holds water but gives it up very slowly.

questions.stem: A hilltop and a valley are both over an unconfined aquifer. The water table roughly follows the land surface. Which statement is correct?

choices.A: A well on the hilltop must be deeper to reach water
choices.B: A well on the hilltop is shallower
choices.C: Both wells have the same depth
choices.D: The water table is flat everywhere
choices.E: Wells in the valley are always dry

questions.explanation: The water table is a subdued copy of the land surface: higher under hills, near the surface in valleys.

questions.stem: Which mineral is the hardest on the Mohs scale (10)?
questions.explanation: Diamond is 10 on the Mohs scale. Corundum is 9, topaz 8, quartz 7.

questions.stem: In the kitchen, table salt is the mineral halite. Which of these is NOT a mineral?
questions.explanation: Coal is made of plant remains (organic), so it is a rock, not a mineral.

questions.stem: In Bowen's reaction series, which mineral crystallizes first from a cooling magma?
questions.explanation: High-temperature minerals such as olivine and Ca-rich plagioclase form first. Quartz forms last.

questions.stem: Salt crystals from a salt shaker look like tiny cubes because halite has
questions.explanation: Halite breaks along planes at right angles, so fragments keep a cube shape.

questions.stem: White crust in a pool or kettle (limescale) is mostly calcite. A drop of vinegar on it would
questions.explanation: Calcite (CaCO₃) reacts with acids, releasing carbon dioxide gas.

questions.stem: A cook finds a mineral that scratches a glass plate (5.5) but is scratched by quartz (7). Its hardness is
questions.explanation: It is harder than glass but softer than quartz.

questions.stem: Which pair of minerals would you most likely find together in the same igneous rock?
questions.explanation: Minerals far apart in Bowen's series do not usually coexist. Olivine reacts with the melt before quartz forms. Quartz and muscovite crystallize late together.

questions.stem: A pressure cooker raises the pressure of the steam inside. On a water phase diagram, what does this do to the boiling point?

choices.C: It raises it, so food cooks at over 100 °C

questions.explanation: The liquid-gas line slopes upward: higher pressure needs a higher temperature to boil.

questions.stem: A granite kitchen counter is an example of an
questions.explanation: Granite forms when magma cools slowly deep underground, giving large visible crystals.

questions.stem: On a volcano map (suppose), lava that cools quickly at the surface forms rock with
questions.explanation: Fast cooling gives atoms little time to build large crystals, as in basalt and obsidian.

questions.stem: A baker rolls dough on a marble slab. Marble forms when which rock is changed by heat and pressure?
questions.explanation: Limestone (calcite) recrystallizes into marble under heat and pressure.

questions.stem: A cook cools sugar syrup slowly and gets big crystals (rock candy). Quickly cooled syrup makes tiny crystals or glass. Which pair of rocks behaves like this?
questions.explanation: Slow cooling underground gives granite's big crystals. Fast cooling at the surface gives basalt's tiny crystals.

questions.stem: A sheet of igneous rock lies parallel to the sedimentary layers around it. It is called a
questions.explanation: A sill goes along the layers, a dike cuts across them.

questions.stem: On a volcano map, suppose one island has gentle, flowing lava while another erupts explosively. The island with gentle lava most likely has magma that is
questions.explanation: Low-silica magma is runny, so gas escapes easily and eruptions are gentle (like Hawaii).

questions.stem: Sandstone shows mud cracks and ripple marks at the same level. What best describes the environment?

choices.E: A shallow area that was sometimes covered by water and sometimes dried out

questions.explanation: Ripple marks need shallow moving water, and mud cracks form when mud dries. Together they suggest a tidal flat or shoreline.

questions.stem: Why are explosive eruptions more common with felsic magma?

choices.B: It is viscous, so gas gets trapped and builds up pressure

questions.explanation: Thick magma does not let gas bubbles escape. When the pressure is released, the gas expands violently.

questions.stem: Which layer of the Earth is liquid?
questions.explanation: The outer core is liquid iron and nickel. It is below the solid mantle and surrounds the solid inner core.

questions.stem: Which seismic wave arrives first at a station?
questions.explanation: P waves are the fastest seismic waves, so they arrive first (P for 'primary').

questions.stem: A normal fault is mostly caused by
questions.explanation: In a normal fault the hanging wall moves down because the crust is being pulled apart.

questions.stem: A seismometer shows S waves arriving 20 s after P waves. P waves travel at 6.0 km/s and S waves at 3.5 km/s. How far away is the earthquake?
You can pass a shout through water like a P wave, but you cannot shake the water sideways and pass that motion along like an S wave. This explains why S waves

choices.E: cannot pass through the liquid outer core

questions.explanation: Liquids cannot support shear. So S waves stop at the outer core, which makes the S-wave shadow zone.

questions.stem: Where is the oldest rock on the sea floor found?

choices.D: In the middle of the Pacific only

questions.explanation: New crust forms at the ridge and spreads away. So age increases with distance from the ridge.

questions.stem: In which soil horizon do clay and dissolved minerals from above often accumulate?
questions.explanation: Water carries clay and minerals down from the A horizon and drops them in the B horizon.

questions.stem: A seismic station is 120° from an earthquake. What direct waves does it receive?

choices.B: Neither P nor S waves (it is in the P shadow zone)

questions.explanation: The P shadow zone is 104°-140° and S waves cannot be detected beyond 104°. So neither direct P nor S arrives.

questions.stem: The Himalayas were pushed up where two continents collided, but there is no deep subduction trench. The best reason is that continental crust

choices.E: is too light (buoyant) to sink into the mantle

questions.explanation: Continental crust is less dense than the mantle, so it resists subduction and crumples into mountains.

questions.stem: In a reverse fault, which statement is correct?

choices.A: The hanging wall moves down because of tension
choices.B: The footwall moves up because of tension
choices.D: The hanging wall moves up relative to the footwall because of compression

questions.explanation: Compression squeezes the crust, pushing the hanging wall up over the footwall.

questions.stem: A baked lasagne has layers like sedimentary rock. In rock layers that have not been disturbed, the oldest layer is
questions.explanation: By the principle of superposition, each layer is laid down on top of older ones.

questions.stem: Suppose a Valorant smoke cloud fades so that half of it is left every 5 s, like a half-life. After 10 s (two half-lives) how much of it remains?
questions.explanation: Each half-life halves the amount: 100% → 50% → 25%.

questions.stem: An igneous dike cuts through three sedimentary layers. The dike is
questions.explanation: A feature that cuts across something must be younger than it (cross-cutting relationships).

questions.stem: A lasagne is built from a bottom layer of pasta, then sauce, pasta, cheese. A chef cuts a slice. By superposition, which layer was added last?

choices.C: They were all made at the same time

questions.explanation: Layers are added in order from the bottom, so the top layer is the youngest.

questions.stem: Archaeologists find a wooden cooking spoon with 12.5% of its original carbon-14. The half-life is 5730 years. How old is it?
questions.explanation: 12.5% = (½)³, so 3 half-lives. 3 × 5730 = 17 190 years.

questions.stem: A rock sample has 1 atom of parent isotope for every 3 atoms of daughter isotope (all daughters came from the parent). The parent half-life is 100 million years. The rock age is
questions.explanation: Parent fraction = 1 ÷ 4 = 25% = (½)², so 2 half-lives = 200 million years.

questions.stem: Layers 1 (bottom) to 3 (top) are tilted. A granite dike cuts layers 1-3. Flat layer 4 lies on top of all of them and is not cut by the dike. What is the order from oldest to youngest?
questions.explanation: The dike cuts 1-3, so they are older. Layer 4 is not cut and lies on the erosion surface, so it is younger than the dike.

questions.stem: Which is the most suitable method to date a 40 000-year-old wooden cooking spoon and a 3-billion-year-old granite?

choices.B: Carbon-14 for the tool and uranium-lead for the granite
choices.E: Uranium-lead for the tool and carbon-14 for the granite

questions.explanation: C-14 (5730 years) fades after about 50 000 years but suits wood. U-238 (4.47 billion years) suits very old rocks.

questions.stem: The orbit of a planet around the Sun is an

choices.A: perfect circle with the Sun at the center
choices.C: ellipse with the Sun at one focus
choices.E: ellipse with the Sun at the center

questions.explanation: This is Kepler's first law.

questions.stem: Where in its orbit does a planet move fastest?
questions.explanation: To sweep equal areas in equal times, the planet must move faster when it is closer to the Sun.

questions.stem: The distance between two masses is doubled. The gravitational force between them becomes
questions.explanation: F ∝ 1 ÷ r². Doubling r makes the force 1 ÷ 4.

questions.stem: An asteroid orbits the Sun with a semi-major axis of 4 AU. Using T² = a³, what is its period?
questions.explanation: T² = 4³ = 64, so T = 8 years.

questions.stem: The hydrogen line has a laboratory wavelength of 656.3 nm. In a star it is measured at 656.6 nm. About how fast is the star moving and in which direction? (c = 3.0 × 10⁵ km/s)
questions.explanation: Δλ = 0.3 nm. v = c × Δλ ÷ λ = 3.0 × 10⁵ × 0.3 ÷ 656.3 ≈ 137 km/s. A longer wavelength is a redshift, so it moves away.

questions.stem: In a binary system, the stars are separated by 2 AU and orbit each other every 2 years. What is the total mass?
questions.explanation: M₁ + M₂ = a³ ÷ T² = 8 ÷ 4 = 2 solar masses.

questions.stem: A comet's orbit takes it to 1 AU from the Sun at perihelion and 9 AU at aphelion. Its orbital period is about
questions.explanation: Semi-major axis a = (1 + 9) ÷ 2 = 5 AU. T² = 5³ = 125, so T ≈ 11.2 years.

questions.stem: Two stars of 3 and 1 solar masses are 4 AU apart. How far is the center of mass from the heavier star?
questions.explanation: The center of mass is closer to the heavier star: r = 4 × 1 ÷ (3 + 1) = 1 AU. The two distances multiply by mass to balance: 1 × 3 = 3 × 1.

questions.stem: A swimmer wears a white cap on a sunny day. White is like a surface with a high albedo, which
questions.explanation: Albedo is the fraction reflected. Fresh snow reflects about 80%.

questions.stem: A gas stove has a blue flame and an electric coil glows dull red. By the same idea (Wien's law), which star looks bluest?
questions.explanation: By Wien's law, hotter stars peak at shorter (bluer) wavelengths.

questions.stem: Which star is brightest in the sky?
questions.explanation: On the magnitude scale, smaller numbers are brighter. -1 is the smallest of these.

questions.stem: Star A has magnitude 1 and star B has magnitude 6. How do their brightnesses compare?

choices.A: A is 5 times brighter than B
choices.C: A is 10 times brighter than B
choices.D: A is 100 times brighter than B
choices.E: B is 100 times brighter than A

questions.explanation: 5 magnitudes equals a factor of 100, and the smaller number is brighter.

questions.stem: The Sun's surface is 5800 K. Using λmax = 2.898 × 10⁻³ m·K ÷ T, at what wavelength does its radiation peak?
questions.explanation: λmax = 2.898 × 10⁻³ ÷ 5800 = 5.0 × 10⁻⁷ m = 500 nm (green-yellow light).

questions.stem: A baker notices a dark baking tray cooks the bottom of cookies faster than a shiny one. The dark tray has a

choices.C: lower albedo, so it absorbs more radiant heat
choices.E: higher albedo, so it reflects more

questions.explanation: Dark surfaces reflect less and absorb more radiation, so they heat up faster.

questions.stem: Star X has twice the radius of star Y and half its surface temperature. How do their luminosities compare (L ∝ R²T⁴)?

choices.C: X is 4 times as luminous as Y
choices.E: X is one quarter as luminous as Y

questions.stem: A planet at 1 AU has albedo 0.30. Its equilibrium temperature is T = 278 K × (1 − albedo)^(1/4). What is it?
Which constellation contains Polaris?
questions.explanation: Polaris is at the end of the handle of the Little Dipper, in Ursa Minor.

questions.stem: Which is the brightest star in the night sky (not counting the Sun)?
questions.explanation: Sirius (α Canis Majoris) has magnitude -1.46.

questions.stem: M31 is the
questions.explanation: M31 is the nearest big spiral galaxy, about 2.5 million light-years away.

questions.stem: A star has a parallax of 0.05 arcseconds. How far away is it?
A swimmer at a night-swim camp at latitude 45° N looks at Polaris. At what altitude above the horizon is Polaris?
questions.explanation: Polaris is almost at the north celestial pole. Its altitude equals the observer's latitude.

questions.stem: A swimmer trains at night in Jakarta (about 6° S). Polaris is
questions.explanation: In the Southern Hemisphere the north celestial pole lies below the horizon, so Polaris cannot be seen from there.

questions.stem: A night-swim camp is at 40° N. Which star is circumpolar there?
questions.explanation: It needs dec > 90° − 40° = 50°. Only +60° meets this.

questions.stem: Swimmers in Jakarta and in London can both see Orion at night because it lies

choices.C: close to the north celestial pole
choices.E: close to the south celestial pole

questions.explanation: The belt of Orion is at about 0° declination, so it is above the horizon for most observers on Earth.

questions.stem: A solar eclipse can only happen at
questions.explanation: The Moon must be between the Sun and Earth for its shadow to fall on Earth.

questions.stem: Which planet is the largest?
questions.explanation: Jupiter has more than twice the mass of all other planets combined.

questions.stem: During a full moon, the Moon is

choices.C: between the Earth and the Sun
choices.D: on the opposite side of Earth from the Sun
choices.E: at a right angle to the Earth-Sun line

questions.explanation: At full moon we see the fully lit side because the Sun lights the face turned toward Earth.

questions.stem: The Moon orbits Earth in 27.32 days relative to the stars, and Earth's year is 365.25 days. What is the synodic month (new moon to new moon)?
Mars orbits the Sun in 1.881 years. About how often does Earth catch up with Mars (synodic period)?
Light needs how long to travel from the Moon (384 400 km away) to Earth? (c = 300 000 km/s)
A full moon occurs on 1 January. About when is the next full moon?
questions.explanation: The synodic month is 29.5 days, so the next full moon is about 30-31 January.

questions.stem: Venus has an orbital period of 0.615 years. How often does it return to the same position relative to Earth and the Sun (synodic period)?
During a total solar eclipse an observer inside the umbra sees

choices.A: only part of the Sun covered
choices.C: the Sun completely covered by the Moon

questions.explanation: Inside the umbra the Moon covers the whole disk of the Sun. In the penumbra the eclipse is only partial.

questions.stem: A Valorant map (suppose) is a mountain 5.5 km high. If the air pressure at the base is 1000 hPa, about what is it at the summit?
questions.explanation: Air pressure roughly halves every 5.5 km of height, so it is about 1000 ÷ 2 = 500 hPa.

questions.stem: A swimmer watches thin clouds thicken slowly over many hours into steady light rain, with a long gentle slope of cloud ahead. Which front is arriving?
questions.explanation: A warm front has a gentle slope and brings widespread steady rain, with clouds lowering slowly.

questions.stem: A cook boils a pot with a lid on. Water drops form on the inside of the lid. This process is
questions.explanation: Hot water vapor touches the cooler lid and turns back into liquid. This is the same process that forms clouds.

questions.stem: At a beach near 45° N, the wind usually blows from the west. Which wind belt is this?
questions.explanation: The westerlies blow between about 30° and 60° latitude, from west to east.

questions.stem: During the day a cooling breeze blows from the sea onto a hot beach. The reason is that

choices.A: land heats faster, so warm air rises over land and cooler sea air flows in
choices.B: land cools faster in the day
choices.C: the Moon pulls the air inland
choices.D: the trade winds blow the other way
choices.E: the sea is warmer than the land, so sea air rises

questions.explanation: Land has a lower heat capacity than water, so it warms more. Rising air over land makes lower pressure, and sea air moves in to replace it.

questions.stem: A Valorant map has a river through the middle (suppose it is 8 m wide, 1 m deep and flows at 2 m/s). What is its discharge?
questions.explanation: Q = width × depth × velocity = 8 × 1 × 2 = 16 m³/s.

questions.stem: It is easier to float in the sea than in a swimming pool because seawater is

choices.A: denser because of the dissolved salt

questions.explanation: Seawater has a density of about 1025 kg/m³, a little higher than fresh water (1000 kg/m³). A denser fluid gives a larger upward force.

questions.stem: On an icy Valorant map, a huge boulder sits alone on a flat plain, far from any rock like it. Geologists call a boulder moved by ice this way an
questions.explanation: A glacier can carry rocks for many kilometers and leave them behind when it melts. They do not match the rock below them.

questions.stem: An empty swimming pool built below the water table can 'pop up' out of the ground. Why?

choices.B: Groundwater pushes up on it with a buoyant force

questions.explanation: Below the water table groundwater pushes up like water pushes up on a boat. An empty pool is light, so it can float up.

questions.stem: A kitchen window is made of glass with hardness about 5.5. Which mineral could scratch it?
questions.explanation: Only a mineral harder than glass (5.5) can scratch it. Quartz at 7 qualifies, the others are too soft.

questions.stem: Some restaurants serve food on slate plates. Slate is a metamorphic rock formed from
questions.explanation: Low-grade heat and pressure change shale (a mudstone) into slate.

questions.stem: In a simmering pot of soup, hot soup rises in the middle and sinks at the edges. In the Earth, this is most like

choices.E: the spin of the outer core

questions.explanation: Heat from the core makes mantle rock rise slowly while cooler rock sinks. These slow currents move the plates. The difference: the mantle is solid and flows over millions of years.

questions.stem: On a layered cliff on a game map (suppose), a conglomerate layer contains pebbles of the sandstone below it. What does this tell you?

choices.A: The sandstone is younger than its pebbles
choices.C: The conglomerate is older than the sandstone
choices.E: The pebbles (sandstone) are older than the conglomerate

questions.explanation: By the principle of inclusions, pieces inside a rock are older than the rock that contains them.

questions.stem: Swimmers doing laps in a small pool finish a lap faster than swimmers in a big pool. In the same way, which planet has the shortest year?

choices.A: All planets have the same year
choices.D: Mercury, the closest to the Sun

questions.explanation: Kepler's third law: the smaller the orbit, the shorter the period (T² = a³). Mercury takes 88 days, Neptune about 165 years.

questions.stem: A cook moves a heat lamp from 30 cm to 60 cm above the food. The heat flux on the food becomes
questions.explanation: Flux follows the inverse-square law. Doubling the distance gives 1 ÷ 2² = 1 ÷ 4 of the flux.

questions.stem: A swimmer on a night swim in Jakarta sees Betelgeuse, the red shoulder of Orion. Betelgeuse looks red because its surface is

choices.D: the same temperature as the Sun

questions.explanation: By Wien's law cool stars peak at longer (redder) wavelengths. Betelgeuse is a red supergiant at about 3500 K.

questions.stem: On an evening in the Northern Hemisphere you see the Moon with its right half lit. Which phase is it?
questions.explanation: A right-lit half Moon in the evening is the first quarter (waxing) Moon, seen after sunset. In the Southern Hemisphere the lit side appears on the left.
